To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the repair of UV light-induced damage in transcribed DNA sequences is the same in cells that have been cultured for different numbers of passages and is the same in young and old individuals.
there is no change in the repair rate of UV damage as a function of aging in human and rat cells, and there is no change as a function of cell passage number in rat embryo fibroblats.
the UV repair of specific transcribable sequences is not altered in human and rat fibroblasts during the aging process.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the repair of UV-induced DNA damage in specific sequences.
the effect of aging on DNA repair.
age-related changes in DNA repair in transcribed sequences.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no age-related alteration in the repair of specific DNA sequences in human or rat fibroblasts.
there is no age-related change, in vitro or in vivo, in the repair of transcribed DNA sequences by UV light-induced damage in human or rat cells.
there is no age-related change of UV-induced DNA damage repair in these cell types.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
no significant alteration in DNA repair was observed in cells from different ages or from different species, nor in cells that were in culture for a long period of time.

there is no age-related change of UV repair of transcribed sequences in human fibroblasts in vitro, in human skin fibroblasts and rat skin fibroblats in vivo, and in rat embryo fibroblats as a function of age.

there are no age-related differences in repair of UV damage, either in the transcribed or the nontranscribed regions of the plasmid, in human fibroblasts, or in the transcribed region of the plasmids in primary cultures of rat fibroblasts and in the nontranscribed region of the same plasmid in rat embryo fibroblastic cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is no evidence for age-related changes in the repair of DNA sequences that are actively transcribed.
UV repair is not a major factor in the aging process.
the repair of UV lesions in transcribed genes is not affected by in vitro aging or by in vivo age in rat fibroblasts.
